post.title: Your checkout needs idempotency keys
post.subtitle: Retries without idempotency do not make a payment flow resilient. They make it charge people twice.

content.text: Every checkout eventually meets the same incident. A payment provider takes too long to answer, the request times out, something retries, and a customer is charged twice. The support ticket arrives before the alert does.

The instinct is to make the timeout longer or to remove the retry. Both are wrong. The retry is the correct behaviour for a distributed system. What is missing is a way for the other side to recognise that it has seen this request before.

A network timeout tells you nothing about what happened on the server. The request may never have arrived. It may have arrived, been processed fully, and had its response lost on the way back. From the caller's point of view these two cases look identical, and they require opposite responses.
This is why retry logic added without thought is dangerous specifically on writes. Reading a product twice is free. Placing an order twice is not.

content.title: The rule worth internalising
content.text: Any operation that creates an order, captures a payment or moves inventory must be safe to call more than once with the same input.
What an idempotency key actually does

An idempotency key is a unique token the **caller** generates and attaches to a write request. The server stores the key alongside the result of the first successful execution. If the same key arrives again, the server skips the work and replays the stored response.

The important detail is that the key is generated by the caller, once, before the first attempt. If the client generates a new key on retry, the mechanism does nothing at all. I have seen that bug ship more than once.

The server side is where most implementations get it subtly wrong. Storing the key after the work completes leaves a window where two concurrent requests with the same key both pass the check. The record has to be claimed before the work starts.
A unique constraint on the key column does this for you. Insert first, and let the database reject the duplicate.

content.code:
CREATE TABLE idempotency_record (
  idempotency_key  VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash     CHAR(64)     NOT NULL,
  state            VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,  -- IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED
  response_body    JSON         NULL,
  created_at       TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

content.text: The flow becomes four steps, and the order of them is the whole design.

items: Insert the key with state `IN_PROGRESS`. A duplicate-key error means someone else got here first.
If the insert failed and the stored record is `COMPLETED`, return the stored response and do no work.
If the insert failed and the record is still `IN_PROGRESS`, return `409 Conflict` so the caller backs off rather than racing.
On success, do the work, then update the record to `COMPLETED` with the response body in the same transaction.

content.text: Storing a hash of the request alongside the key protects against a real client bug: reusing a key for a different payload. If the key matches but the hash does not, the correct answer is an error rather than a replayed response. Returning the old response in that case hides the bug and produces a wrong order.

content.title: On expiry
content.text: Keys do not need to live forever. Twenty-four hours covers every legitimate retry window I have needed. Expire them on a schedule so the table does not grow without bound.

On a headless migration I worked on, fraud verification and payment capture both sat on the synchronous checkout path. Moving verification to asynchronous processing cut the latency, but it also widened the window in which a retry could arrive. Idempotency keys were what made that change safe rather than merely faster.
The pattern costs a table, a unique constraint and about an afternoon. It removes an entire category of incident, permanently. There are not many trades in backend engineering that good.
